Play and get experience. I developed all of my techniques from trial and error, and I think ultimately that made me better than looking up guides and following them to the tee. I tried out a lot more than simply following guidelines.

jrobi has good youtube videos. Pick up one opening for white and one defense for black to begin with. I suggest the King's Indian Attack for white and the French defense for black. After that, focus on pattern recognition and tactics. Train yourself to always be thinking about what your opponent's intentions are when he moves a piece. When you learn how to break down his plan, you'll start being able to plan moves to stop it.

One of the tips I got early on that served me quite well: Get a collection of game notation logs (you can often find them in the paper or whole collections in bookstores/libraries). Put a piece of paper over it so only the first row is exposed. Now play out the game as it happened, exposing each line one at a time. Between moves ask yourself what you would do here. You'll be alone and under no pressure, so really, REALLY take your time and consider it. Then reveal the actual move and spend some time considering why that was the move taken.

It was great for me as a kid, because like you, I didn't have anyone to play against and it really forced me to analyze my game and my chess-thinking.

I'll share a little trap I learned a few years ago (that comes up often enough to remember): If an enemy bishop smashes into your pawn at the edge of the board after you've castled, you can often move the adjacent pawn up one space, trapping the piece until you can get around to capturing it. This usually occurs when your king has been forced to move towards the center of the board, and leaves the outermost pawn unguarded. However, once you push the pawn up, its typically protected by the pawn adjacent to it (which in turn is usually still protected by the king).

Tactics, tactics, tactics.

Tactics, as you probably know, are just problems where it's one side to move and usually win. Your goal is to find the optimal moves. Why? You're never going to get that exact position in a regular game after all. The reason is that in order to make meaningful progress at chess you ultimately need to form a subconscious intuition. Doing tactics and even repeating the same tactical problems helps build this subconscious intuition. They also help you formulate "board vision." When a strong player plays chess there is no need for any sort of conscious consideration of which pieces are hanging or anything like that. It's completely intuitive. This is a matter of board vision. This is the reason when you see a strong player play a 3 minute game it might just seem incredible. It's not. It's still crap chess. The only difference is that that's not as readily apparent as they've stopped hanging pieces!

If you were to think of chess as a language then tactics are essentially the grammar of the language. You might be able to able to formulate incredible ideas in your mind but without the tactics to string everything together it's all going to come out garbled and frequently nonsensical. The reason that most folks get stuck at a lower tier of ability is largely because tactics don't actually give you any indication of when they start "working." Spend your time memorizing some opening and you can actually see that play out on the board. It feels good. Stick a copy of "How to Reassess Your Chess" on your throne and the lovely writing of Silman will leave you feeling like you have a lot to chew on, almost like you've had a major breakthrough. It feels good. Go work through a tactics book several times over and erm.. what now?

I also would not recommend online tactics trainers like at chess.com, chess.emrald.net, etc. The reason is two fold. The first is that those problems are computer solved. So let's take a fairly common situation. The first obvious move of a tactics problem leads to a very complex but ultimately forced mate, unless black immediately tosses his queen for a pawn. In a computer checked problem the computer will choose the optimal defense which is throwing away his queen. So you play the one obvious move, black gives away his queen, and it moves onto the next problem. You just missed out on 99% of the problem. Another issue is that it encourages laziness. I was discussing a recent tactics problem with a student of mine and he actually solved it substantially faster than I had. Of course he hadn't actually solved it at all. He'd simply kept picking standard tactical ideas until he worked his way through the position in slightly more intelligent than brute force fashion. You're going to get 0 benefit from doing that.

So how should you study tactics? Grab a book. I'd recommend a classic: Fred Reinfeld's 1001 Winning Chess Sacrifices and Combinations. Get the book, do an entire page writing down your entire solution and all possible reasonable defenses, and only then check it. And move on. When you do a later chapter go back and briefly redo earlier chapters mentally. This is hard work and most people will not consider it particularly fun, but if you complete it you'd see your results skyrocket.
